modules.title: Complex Sentence Structures
modules.description: Master relative clauses, reported speech, passive voice in all tenses, and mixed conditionals — essential for clear, sophisticated communication at the upper-intermediate level.

lessons.title: Relative Clauses
lessons.description: Learn defining and non-defining relative clauses, relative pronouns, and preposition stranding.

body.html:
Relative clauses give extra information about a noun. Choosing between defining and non-defining clauses changes meaning.

Defining Relative Clauses

A defining clause identifies which person or thing we mean. Without it, the sentence is incomplete. No commas.

  • The engineer who designed this API works at Google.
  • Code that is not covered by tests is risky to refactor.
  • The commit which broke the build was reverted immediately.

Non-Defining Relative Clauses

Adds extra, non-essential information. The sentence makes sense without it. Commas required. Cannot use 'that'.

  • Spring Boot, which was released in 2014, is the most popular Java framework.
  • Our CTO, who has a PhD in Machine Learning, presented the keynote.
  • The legacy monolith, which we are decomposing, has been running since 2010.

Relative Pronouns

  • who — people (subject/object): the developer who wrote this
  • whom — people (object, formal): the colleague whom I consulted
  • which — things: the framework which we adopted
  • that — people/things in DEFINING clauses only: the bug that caused the outage
  • whose — possession: the engineer whose PR broke the build
  • where/when — place/time: the sprint where we shipped v2
tips: In defining clauses, you can OMIT the relative pronoun if it is the OBJECT: 'the API (that) we built' is correct.
After prepositions, use 'which' (not 'that'): 'the conference at which she spoke'. In speech: 'the conference she spoke at'.
Non-defining clauses ALWAYS have commas and NEVER use 'that'.

body.question: The microservice, ___ was deployed last week, handles payment processing.

body.sentence: The conference ___ which she presented was fully virtual.
body.explanation: Formal: preposition before 'which'. Informal: 'the conference she presented at'.

lessons.title: Reported Speech & Reporting Verbs
lessons.description: Master tense-shift rules and advanced reporting verb patterns for technical communication.

body.html:
When reporting past speech, tenses move one step back (backshift).

Backshift Chart

DirectReported
Present Simple: "The API is down."She said the API was down.
Past Simple: "The build failed."She said the build had failed.
Present Perfect: "We have deployed v3."He said they had deployed v3.
Will: "The fix will be ready."She said the fix would be ready.
Can: "We can scale."He said they could scale.

Advanced Reporting Verbs

  • Verb + that: admit, claim, explain, insist, recommend, suggest
  • Verb + object + infinitive: advise, encourage, persuade, urge, warn
  • Verb + gerund: deny, mention, propose, report, suggest

He admitted that the outage was caused by a misconfiguration.

She recommended that we adopt blue-green deployment. (subjunctive: 'adopt' not 'adopts')
tips: With 'suggest/recommend', use subjunctive base form: 'I suggest that he monitor the logs.'
Reported questions use STATEMENT word order: 'She asked what the status was' (not 'was the status').
For yes/no questions, use 'if' or 'whether'.

body.question: Direct: 'Why did the pipeline fail?' → She asked ___.
body.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order with tense backshift.

body.sentence: The SRE ___ (recommend) that we ___ (use) a canary deployment.
body.explanation: After 'recommend that', use subjunctive base form (use, not uses/used).

lessons.title: Passive Voice in Depth
lessons.description: Use passive constructions in all tenses, with modal verbs, and impersonal passive — critical for technical documentation.

body.html:
The passive is essential in technical writing when the agent is unknown or deliberately omitted.

Passive in All Tenses (be + past participle)

  • Present: The service is deployed automatically.
  • Present Continuous: v2 is being rolled out.
  • Past: A bug was introduced.
  • Present Perfect: The issue has been patched.
  • Future: The API will be released next sprint.

Passive with Modals

  • Data must be encrypted at rest and in transit.
  • This endpoint should be rate-limited.
  • The service can be scaled horizontally.

Get-Passive (Informal)

For unexpected/negative events: Our server got hacked last night.

Impersonal Passive (Formal/Academic)

It + be + past participle + that clause:

  • It is assumed that the data is normally distributed.
  • It has been shown that this architecture scales linearly.
tips: In technical docs, prefer passive when agent is obvious: 'The container is orchestrated by Kubernetes.'
Passive with 'by' is rare — only use it when the agent is surprising or critical.
Avoid double passives: 'The code is attempted to be compiled' is wrong.

body.translation: All sensitive data must be encrypted.

body.question: Which is the correct impersonal passive?
options: It is believed that the system is secure.
It believes that the system is secure.
The system is believed that is secure.
It is believing the system is secure.
body.explanation: It + be + past participle + that clause.

lessons.title: Mixed Conditionals, Wish & Alternatives
lessons.description: Express regret, hypothetical past-present connections, and alternatives to 'if'.

body.html:
Mixed Conditional: Past Condition → Present Result

If + past perfect, would + infinitive

  • If I had studied CS, I would be a developer now.
  • If we had adopted microservices earlier, the system wouldn't be so hard to maintain.

Mixed Conditional: Present Condition → Past Result

If + past simple, would have + past participle

  • If she were more experienced, she would have caught that race condition.

Wish / If Only

  • wish + past simple — present regret: I wish I understood quantum computing.
  • wish + past perfect — past regret: I wish I had learned Docker earlier.
  • wish + would — frustration/desire for change: I wish the CI pipeline would run faster.

Alternatives to 'If'

  • Unless (= if not): Deployment fails unless all tests pass.
  • As long as / Provided that: Deploy as long as tests pass.
  • Supposing: Supposing the DB goes down — what's the plan?
  • Otherwise: We need caching, otherwise the API will time out.
tips: 'If only' is stronger than 'wish': 'If only I had monitored the logs!'
In formal writing, use 'were' for all subjects: 'If I were the architect...'
After 'wish', NEVER use present tense.

body.question: If I ___ that course on distributed systems last year, I ___ a better architect now.
body.explanation: Mixed: past perfect (past action) + would + infinitive (present result).

body.sentence: I wish I ___ (learn) about clean architecture patterns earlier.
body.explanation: Wish + past perfect expresses regret about the past.

flashcardDecks.title: B2 Grammar Patterns
flashcardDecks.description: 25 essential B2 grammar patterns: relative clauses, reported speech, passive voice, and conditionals.

front.text: defining relative clause

back.text: Identifies which person/thing — NO commas. Essential to meaning.
back.example: The PR that broke the build was reverted.
back.notes: Can use that/which/who. Object pronouns can be omitted.

front.text: non-defining relative clause

back.text: Adds extra, non-essential info — WITH commas. Cannot use 'that'.
back.example: Kubernetes, which was developed at Google, orchestrates containers.
back.notes: Always commas. Only who/which/whose. Never omit pronoun.

front.text: preposition + which (formal relative)

back.text: Formal relative: preposition placed before 'which' or 'whom'.
back.example: The meeting at which she presented was recorded.
back.notes: Informal: 'the meeting she presented at'. Never 'that' after preposition.

front.text: reported speech — backshift

back.text: Tenses move one step back when reporting past speech.
back.example: 'The API is down' → She said the API was down.
back.notes: Present→Past, Past→Past Perfect, Will→Would. No shift if still true.

front.text: subjunctive after suggest/recommend

back.text: Use BASE form of verb in that-clause after suggest/recommend/insist.
back.example: I recommend that he deploy the fix. (NOT 'deploys')
back.notes: Formal English. Common in technical proposals and specifications.

front.text: passive voice — all tenses

back.text: be + past participle. Focuses on action/receiver, not doer.
back.example: The database was migrated last night.
back.notes: Essential in technical docs. Agent with 'by' is optional.

front.text: passive with modals

back.example: All requests must be authenticated.
back.notes: Common in security requirements and API specs.

front.text: impersonal passive

back.text: It + be + past participle + that clause. Formal/academic.
back.example: It is assumed that the data is accurate.
back.notes: Verbs: assume, believe, claim, expect, report, show.

front.text: get-passive

back.text: get + past participle — informal, for unexpected/negative events.
back.example: The server got hacked over the weekend.
back.notes: More common in speech. Not for formal writing.

front.text: mixed conditional: past → present

back.text: If + past perfect, would + infinitive. Past action changes present.
back.example: If I had learned Terraform, I would deploy infrastructure now.
back.notes: Bridges time frames: past condition, present result.

front.text: mixed conditional: present → past

back.text: If + past simple, would have + pp. Present state explains past outcome.
back.example: If I were more experienced, I would have caught that bug.
back.notes: Current trait affecting a past event.

front.text: wish + past simple

back.text: Regret about the PRESENT. Past form, present meaning.
back.example: I wish I knew Go. (But I don't.)
back.notes: Never present tense after wish. 'I wish I know' is WRONG.

front.text: wish + past perfect

back.example: I wish I had monitored the memory usage.
back.notes: Common in post-mortems: 'I wish we had caught this earlier.'

front.text: wish + would

back.text: Frustration or desire for someone/something to change.
back.example: I wish the CI pipeline would run faster.
back.notes: Cannot use for yourself: NOT 'I wish I would'.

front.text: unless

back.example: The deployment fails unless all tests pass.
back.notes: Don't add 'not' — unless already contains negation.

front.text: provided that / as long as

back.example: You can deploy as long as all tests pass.
back.notes: Formal. Common in contracts and technical requirements.

front.text: otherwise

back.text: Introduces consequence if condition is NOT met.
back.example: We need caching — otherwise the API will time out.
back.notes: Risk documentation pattern. = 'if not, then...'

front.text: supposing

back.text: Introduces a hypothetical scenario for discussion.
back.example: Supposing the primary region fails — how does failover work?
back.notes: DR planning and architecture discussions.

front.text: reported questions — word order

back.text: Reported questions use STATEMENT word order, no inversion.
back.example: She asked why the deployment had failed.
back.notes: NOT 'had the deployment failed'. If/whether for yes/no.

front.text: reporting verb + gerund

back.example: He denied having introduced the memory leak.
back.notes: Formal pattern. 'Denied introducing' is also correct.

front.text: reporting verb + object + infinitive

back.example: The SRE warned us to monitor memory usage.
back.notes: Common in guidance, alerts, and recommendations.

front.text: passive — future perfect

back.text: will have been + past participle — done before a future point.
back.example: The migration will have been completed by Q3.
back.notes: Project timeline language.

front.text: if only

back.example: If only we had implemented circuit breakers!
back.notes: Same grammar as wish. Stronger regret.

front.text: would rather + past

back.text: Preference about someone else's action. Past form, present meaning.
back.example: I'd rather you didn't push to production on Friday.
back.notes: Polite, indirect. Formal alternative to 'don't'.

front.text: object relative pronoun omission

back.text: In DEFINING clauses, omit relative pronoun if it is the OBJECT.
back.example: The API (which) we built handles 10k rps.
back.notes: Only defining clauses. Only when pronoun is object.

modules.title: Technical & Professional Lexicon
modules.description: Build your technical vocabulary for Java backend development, software engineering practices, AI/ML fundamentals, and cloud infrastructure.

lessons.title: Java Backend Terminology
lessons.description: Master the key terms used in Java backend development: frameworks, patterns, and JVM concepts.

body.html:
Core Frameworks & Runtime

  • Spring Boot — Opinionated framework for production-ready Spring apps with auto-configuration and embedded servers.
  • dependency injection (DI) — Objects receive dependencies from a container rather than creating them. Spring's core concept.
  • inversion of control (IoC) — The principle behind DI: the framework controls flow, not your code. 'Don't call us, we'll call you.'
  • bean — In Spring, any object managed by the IoC container.
  • JPA / Hibernate — JPA = specification, Hibernate = implementation for object-relational mapping.

API & Communication

  • REST — Architectural style using HTTP methods and resources.
  • DTO — Data Transfer Object. Plain object carrying data between layers.
  • serialization — Converting objects to JSON/XML/binary for transmission. Jackson is the standard.
  • middleware — Software handling cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, rate limiting).

Data & Persistence

  • connection pool — Cache of DB connections for reuse. HikariCP is standard in Spring Boot.
  • transaction (ACID) — Atomic unit of work. Managed via @Transactional.
tips: Spring Boot's 'opinionated' nature means it makes choices for you — you can override them.
JPA is the spec (the 'what'), Hibernate is the implementation (the 'how').
DTOs should be dumb — no business logic, just fields and getters/setters.

body.question: In Spring, an object managed by the IoC container is called a ___.
body.explanation: A 'bean' is any object managed by the Spring IoC container.

body.sentence: ___ ___ is a pattern where an object receives its dependencies from outside rather than creating them.
body.explanation: DI is Spring's foundational concept. Dependencies are injected by the framework.

lessons.title: Software Engineering Practices
lessons.description: Vocabulary for modern software development: CI/CD, testing, design patterns, and code quality.

body.html:
CI/CD

  • continuous integration (CI) — Frequently merging code with automated builds and tests.
  • continuous delivery/deployment (CD) — Automating release so software can be deployed any time.
  • pipeline — Automated sequence (build → test → scan → deploy).
  • canary release — Deploy to small user subset first, then gradually roll out.
  • blue-green deployment — Two identical environments, switch traffic instantly.

Testing & Quality

  • unit test — Tests single code unit in isolation. Foundation of test pyramid.
  • integration test — Tests multiple components working together.
  • regression — Bug where previously working feature breaks after a change.
  • code coverage — Percentage of code executed during testing. 100% != bug-free.
  • static analysis — Analyzing code without executing (SonarQube, Checkstyle).

Process

  • code review / peer review — Another developer examines your code before merge.
  • pull request (PR) — Request to merge branch into main. Unit of code review.
  • tech debt — Short-term expedient code creating long-term maintenance costs.
tips: CI without CD is like baking a cake and never serving it.
Test coverage != test quality. 100% with weak assertions is worthless.
Code review is primarily about knowledge sharing, not just bug finding.

body.translation: Build → Test → Scan → Deploy (typical CI/CD pipeline).

body.sentence: Accumulated ___ ___ slows down velocity and increases maintenance costs.
body.explanation: Tech debt = code written quickly without proper design, creating future rework costs.

lessons.title: AI & Machine Learning Fundamentals
lessons.description: Essential vocabulary for discussing AI/ML: from training paradigms to model architecture and evaluation.

body.html:
Learning Paradigms

  • supervised learning — Training on labeled data (input → correct output). Classification, regression.
  • unsupervised learning — Finding patterns in unlabeled data. Clustering, anomaly detection.
  • reinforcement learning (RL) — Agent learns by interacting with environment, receiving rewards/penalties.

Model Architecture & Training

  • neural network — Interconnected layers of nodes inspired by biological neurons.
  • transformer — Dominant NLP architecture using self-attention. Powers GPT, BERT, Claude.
  • fine-tuning — Training a pre-trained model further on specific data. Much cheaper than from scratch.
  • embedding — Dense vector representing data in continuous space. Foundation of semantic search and RAG.
  • token — Unit of text a language model processes (~4 characters in English).

Evaluation

  • overfitting — Model memorizes training data, fails on new data. The #1 ML problem.
  • precision / recall — Precision = accuracy of positive predictions. Recall = completeness of finding positives.
  • F1 score — Harmonic mean of precision and recall.
  • ground truth — The verified correct answer for comparison.
tips: Fine-tuning adjusts weights that already encode language understanding — like teaching a fluent speaker a new topic.
Embeddings are the 'secret sauce' of modern AI apps. Vector similarity enables semantic search.
In production ML, the model is ~5% of the system. The rest is data, infra, monitoring, retraining.

body.question: When a model performs well on training data but poorly on unseen data, it is ___.
body.explanation: Overfitting = memorized training data instead of learning general patterns.

body.sentence: Word ___ convert text into dense vectors, enabling semantic similarity search.
body.explanation: Embeddings are vector representations. 'car' and 'automobile' have similar vectors.

lessons.title: Data Infrastructure & Cloud
lessons.description: Vocabulary for databases, caching, messaging, containers, and cloud-native infrastructure.

body.html:
Compute & Containers

  • container — Lightweight unit packaging code and dependencies. Docker is standard.
  • orchestration — Automating deployment, scaling, management of containers. Kubernetes is standard.
  • serverless — Cloud model: write functions, provider manages servers. Pay per invocation.

Data Storage

  • RDBMS — Relational database with tables and SQL. PostgreSQL, MySQL.
  • NoSQL — Non-relational: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), column-family (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j).
  • caching — Storing frequent data in fast memory. Redis, Memcached.
  • sharding — Splitting database across servers for horizontal scaling.

Messaging & Streaming

  • message broker — Routes messages between producers/consumers. RabbitMQ, SQS.
  • event streaming — Continuous flow of immutable events. Apache Kafka is standard.

Observability

  • metrics, logs, traces — The three pillars: what's happening, why, and where.
tips: Three pillars: metrics (what), logs (why), traces (where).
Caching is a trade-off: speed vs. staleness. Define your invalidation strategy.
Kubernetes is an orchestrator, not a container runtime (containerd/CRI-O underneath).

body.question: Which is NOT one of the three pillars of observability?
body.explanation: The three pillars are metrics, logs, traces. Alerting is built ON TOP of observability.

body.sentence: Apache ___ is a distributed event streaming platform for real-time data pipelines.
body.explanation: Kafka enables pub/sub messaging with persistent storage and replay.

flashcardDecks.title: B2 Technical Vocabulary — Core
flashcardDecks.description: 25 essential technical terms: Java backend, software engineering, AI/ML, and cloud infrastructure.

front.text: dependency injection

back.text: Objects receive dependencies from a container rather than instantiating them directly.
back.example: Spring uses DI to wire together components.
back.notes: Core Spring concept. Reduces coupling, improves testability.

front.text: inversion of control (IoC)

back.text: Framework controls program flow — 'Don't call us, we'll call you.'
back.example: Spring's IoC container manages bean lifecycles.
back.notes: DI is the most common implementation of IoC.

front.text: bean (Spring)

back.text: Any object managed by the Spring IoC container.
back.example: @Service, @Repository, @Component classes become beans.
back.notes: Singletons by default. Managed end-to-end by the container.

front.text: DTO

back.text: Data Transfer Object. Plain object with no business logic for transporting data.
back.example: The controller maps requests to a DTO before service layer.
back.notes: Should be flat and simple. Decouples API contract from domain model.

front.text: serialization

back.text: Converting an object to a format for storage or transmission.
back.example: Jackson serializes Java objects to JSON for REST responses.
back.notes: Deserialization is the reverse. JSON is dominant for web APIs.

front.text: transaction (ACID)

back.text: Atomic unit of work that must be atomic, consistent, isolated, durable.
back.example: @Transactional ensures all-or-nothing execution.
back.notes: Key for data integrity. Spring handles declaratively.

front.text: continuous integration (CI)

back.text: Frequently merging code with automated build and test verification.
back.example: Our CI pipeline runs tests on every push.
back.notes: Goal: catch integration issues early. Paired with CD.

front.text: canary release

back.text: Deploying to a small user subset first, then gradually rolling out.
back.example: We canaried v2 to 5% of users before full rollout.
back.notes: Reduces blast radius. Named after 'canary in a coal mine'.

front.text: tech debt

back.text: Short-term expedient code increasing long-term maintenance cost.
back.example: Skipping tests to meet a deadline creates tech debt.
back.notes: Coined by Ward Cunningham. Managed through refactoring.

front.text: regression

back.text: A bug where a previously working feature breaks after a change.
back.example: The refactoring caused a regression in payments.
back.notes: Regression testing aims to catch these.

front.text: neural network

back.text: Computing system of interconnected nodes in layers, inspired by biological brains.
back.example: A deep neural network has many hidden layers.
back.notes: Foundation of deep learning. CNN (vision), Transformer (language).

front.text: fine-tuning

back.text: Training a pre-trained model further on a specific dataset.
back.example: We fine-tuned GPT-4 on our internal documentation.
back.notes: Much cheaper than from scratch. Base model already understands language.

front.text: embedding

back.text: Dense vector representing data in continuous space. Similar items are close.
back.example: 'car' and 'automobile' have similar embedding vectors.
back.notes: Foundation of RAG and semantic search. Word2Vec, BERT, ada-002.

front.text: overfitting

back.text: Model memorizes training data instead of learning patterns — fails on new data.
back.example: 99% training accuracy, 60% test accuracy = classic overfitting.
back.notes: Solutions: regularization, dropout, more data, early stopping.

front.text: precision and recall

back.text: Precision = accuracy of positives. Recall = completeness of finding positives.
back.example: Fraud detection optimizes for recall over precision.
back.notes: F1 = harmonic mean. Trade-off based on business cost of errors.

front.text: orchestration (containers)

back.text: Automating deployment, scaling, management of containerized apps.
back.example: Kubernetes orchestrates microservices across nodes.
back.notes: K8s handles scheduling, service discovery, load balancing, self-healing.

front.text: message broker

back.text: Middleware routing messages between producers and consumers asynchronously.
back.example: RabbitMQ brokers messages between order and inventory services.
back.notes: Enables event-driven architectures. Pub/sub, point-to-point.

front.text: event streaming

back.text: Continuous ordered flow of immutable events — storable and replayable.
back.example: Kafka streams user activity events for real-time analytics.
back.notes: Different from message queues: events are persistent. Kafka dominates.

front.text: caching

back.text: Storing frequent data in fast temporary storage to reduce latency.
back.example: Redis caches API responses with a 5-minute TTL.
back.notes: Trade-off: speed vs. freshness. Challenge: cache invalidation.

front.text: sharding

back.text: Horizontally partitioning data across multiple database instances.
back.example: User data is sharded by user_id across 16 nodes.
back.notes: Key challenge: choosing the shard key. Uneven = 'hot shards'.

front.text: distributed tracing

back.text: Tracking a request across microservices, measuring latency at each hop.
back.example: Jaeger traces showed the bottleneck in inventory service.
back.notes: Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry. Essential for debugging latency.

front.text: serverless

back.text: Cloud model: write functions, provider manages servers. Pay per invocation.
back.example: AWS Lambda handles image processing with zero idle cost.
back.notes: Not actually 'no servers' — just not your problem.

front.text: static analysis

back.text: Analyzing source code without executing to find bugs and vulnerabilities.
back.example: SonarQube runs static analysis on every PR.
back.notes: Shift-left: catch issues early. Different from dynamic analysis.

front.text: token (LLM)

back.text: Unit of text an LLM processes — ~4 characters or 0.75 words in English.
back.example: GPT-4 Turbo has a 128k token context window.
back.notes: Pricing and limits are per token. Varies by model and language.

front.text: ground truth

back.text: The verified correct answer for comparing model predictions against.
back.example: Human annotators created ground truth labels.
back.notes: Quality of ground truth = quality of evaluation. Garbage in, garbage out.

modules.title: Academic & Technical Phrasal Verbs
modules.description: Phrasal verbs that appear frequently in academic papers, technical documentation, and professional engineering discussions.

lessons.title: Academic Phrasal Verbs
lessons.description: Phrasal verbs for research papers, technical reports, and academic presentations.

body.html:
• bear out — to confirm/support: The results bear out our hypothesis.
  • draw on — to use as resource: The architecture draws on DDD principles.
  • put forward — to propose: The paper puts forward a novel approach.
  • account for — to explain cause or represent proportion: Caching accounts for 60% of the improvement.
  • stem from — to originate from: The outage stemmed from a misconfigured LB.
  • rule out — to eliminate as possibility: We ruled out network latency.
  • point to — to indicate as evidence: Metrics point to a memory leak.
tips: 'Account for' has two meanings: (1) explain, (2) constitute a percentage. Context decides.
'Bear out' = evidence confirms. Opposite: 'go against' or 'contradict'.

body.question: The data ___ the hypothesis that caching reduces latency.
body.explanation: 'Bear out' = confirm/support. The data CONFIRMS the hypothesis.

body.sentence: The memory leak ___ (originate from) an unclosed connection.
body.explanation: Stem from = originate from. Common in post-mortems.

lessons.title: Phrasal Verbs in Tech Contexts
lessons.description: Phrasal verbs for deploying, troubleshooting, and managing systems.

body.html:
• spin up — create and start (server, container): Spin up a staging instance.
  • tear down — destroy/remove infrastructure: Tear down test envs to save costs.
  • roll out — deploy gradually: We rolled out the auth middleware to 25%.
  • roll back — revert to previous version: The release was rolled back.
  • scale out — add more instances (horizontal): Scaled out from 3 to 10 pods.
  • scale up — make instances bigger (vertical): Scaled up to larger VMs.
  • bring up — start service/system: Docker Compose brings up the stack.
  • shut down — stop gracefully: Node was shut down for maintenance.
tips: Scale OUT = horizontal (more servers). Scale UP = vertical (bigger servers). Almost always scale OUT.
'Roll back' ≠ 'revert'. Rollback = deployment action. Revert = Git action.

body.translation: We rolled out the new feature.

body.question: Adding more identical servers is called ___.
body.explanation: Scale out = horizontal scaling (more instances). Scale up = vertical (bigger instance).

lessons.title: Professional Communication Phrasal Verbs
lessons.description: Phrasal verbs for meetings, code reviews, design discussions, and professional email.

body.html:
• walk through — explain step by step: Walk me through the architecture.
  • talk over — discuss thoroughly: Let's talk over the trade-offs.
  • flesh out — add detail: We need to flesh out the error-handling strategy.
  • boil down to — reduce to essence: It boils down to an N+1 query.
  • iron out — resolve problems: Ironing out the last few bugs.
  • zero in on — focus precisely: The profiler helped us zero in on the bottleneck.
  • sign off on — give official approval: Architect must sign off on the design.
  • push back on — resist/challenge: Engineering pushed back on the timeline.
tips: 'Walk through' is a noun when hyphenated: 'a walk-through'. Verb: 'walk through'.
'Boil down to' is great for root cause summaries.
'Push back' is constructive — advocating for quality, not being difficult.

body.sentence: After hours of debugging, the issue ___ to a single missing semicolon.
body.explanation: Boil down to = essential core conclusion after removing extraneous details.

body.question: When engineers 'push back on' a deadline, they are ___.
body.explanation: Push back on = challenge constructively, advocating for quality and realistic expectations.

flashcardDecks.title: B2 Academic & Tech Phrasal Verbs
flashcardDecks.description: 20 essential phrasal verbs for academic writing, technical docs, and professional communication.

front.text: bear out

back.text: To confirm or support with evidence.
back.example: The benchmarks bore out our caching assumption.
back.notes: Formal. Evidence validates a claim.

front.text: draw on

back.text: To use knowledge, experience, or existing work as a resource.
back.example: The solution draws on DDD principles.
back.notes: Formal. Common in papers. Inseparable.

front.text: put forward

back.text: To propose, suggest, or present a theory, plan, or argument.
back.example: She put forward a compelling case for Rust.
back.notes: Separable. Formal synonym for 'propose'.

front.text: account for

back.text: (1) To explain. (2) To constitute a percentage.
back.example: Caching accounts for 40% of latency reduction.
back.notes: Inseparable. Two distinct meanings.

front.text: stem from

back.text: To originate from; to be caused by.
back.example: The outage stemmed from a misconfigured firewall.
back.notes: Inseparable. Common in post-mortems.

front.text: rule out

back.text: To eliminate as a possibility; to exclude.
back.example: We ruled out network latency after tracing.
back.notes: Separable. Common in debugging and diagnostics.

front.text: spin up

back.text: To create and start a server, container, or environment.
back.example: Spin up a staging instance to reproduce the bug.
back.notes: Informal DevOps. Formal: 'provision'.

front.text: tear down

back.text: To destroy or remove infrastructure or environments.
back.example: Terraform tears down staging nightly.
back.notes: Separable. Opposite of 'spin up'.

front.text: roll out

back.text: To deploy or release software gradually.
back.example: We rolled out v2 to 10% of users first.
back.notes: Separable. Opposite: 'roll back'.

front.text: roll back

back.text: To revert to a previous version during deployment.
back.example: The release was rolled back after error spike.
back.notes: Separable. Deployment action, not Git revert.

front.text: scale out

back.text: To increase capacity by adding more instances (horizontal).
back.example: The API scaled out from 5 to 20 pods.
back.notes: Horizontal scaling. Preferred in cloud-native.

front.text: bring up

back.text: (1) To start a service. (2) To introduce a topic.
back.example: docker compose up brings up the full stack.
back.notes: Separable. Both DevOps and meeting contexts.

front.text: walk through

back.text: To explain step by step; to guide through a process.
back.example: Walk me through the deployment pipeline.
back.notes: Noun: 'walk-through'. Verb: two words.

front.text: flesh out

back.text: To add detail, substance, or completeness to an idea.
back.example: Flesh out the error-handling section.
back.notes: Separable. From 'adding flesh to a skeleton'.

front.text: boil down to

back.text: To reduce to the essential element; the core conclusion.
back.example: It boils down to a consistency vs. availability trade-off.
back.notes: Inseparable (three-part). Root cause summaries.

front.text: zero in on

back.text: To focus attention precisely on a target or problem.
back.example: The profiler helped us zero in on the hot path.
back.notes: Inseparable (three-part). Debugging context.

front.text: iron out

back.text: To resolve problems or difficulties through effort.
back.example: Ironing out the last integration issues.
back.notes: Separable. Metaphor: smoothing wrinkles.

front.text: sign off on

back.text: To give official approval or authorization.
back.example: Security must sign off on the architecture.
back.notes: Inseparable (three-part). Formal authorization.

front.text: push back on

back.example: Engineering pushed back on the launch date.
back.notes: Inseparable (three-part). Quality advocacy.

front.text: come down to

back.text: To depend on a single decisive factor.
back.example: The decision comes down to cost vs. performance.
back.notes: Inseparable (three-part). Ultimate deciding factor.
